system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2188-12-04 19:02:00 to 2188-12-09 17:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with metastatic breast cancer and refractory gastroparesis was admitted due to a clogged G-tube that ruptured, causing leakage of contents and a chemical skin rash. She developed worsening nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. A new 16 French GJ tube was placed, but it clogged again, requiring replacement with an 18 French tube. During admission, she was diagnosed with recurrent C. difficile infection, treated with oral vancomycin. Skin irritation around the tube site was managed with mupirocin and betamethasone cream. Tube feeds were resumed with Osmolite 1.5, which she tolerated well. She improved clinically, with resolution of symptoms and stable vitals, and was discharged home with services to complete her vancomycin course and continue home care.
problems: Enterocolitis due to Clostridium difficile, recurrent
Secondary malignant neoplasm of liver and intrahepatic bile duct
Irritant contact dermatitis due to other chemical products
Adverse effect of other opioids, initial encounter
Acquired absence of other specified parts of digestive tract
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of breast

left right renal cyst again noted. Cord signal abnormality: no

""history of left breast cancer.  She

an

After her successful reexcision, she had breast conserving

An Oncotype recurrence score was obtained and was 20.  This

results given the fact that this is a lobular tumor and we would
plan to use an aromatase inhibitor.

mastectomy.  Accordingly, anastrozole was started in ___

She spent the winters in ___ and felt relatively well there,
although she did have some back and hip discomfort in ___ that was considered like degenerative.

When she returned this past ___, she was experiencing some
nausea and vomiting as well as abdominal discomfort that was
initially
attributed to her comorbidity of gastroparesis.  During a CT 
scan
to evaluate this, probable numerous hepatic and skeletal
metastases were imaged.  

She was admitted to the hospital and underwent a liver biopsy
showing an estrogen receptor positive carcinoma compatible with 
a
breast primary tumor.  HER-2 was not reassessed but was negative
on her ___ mastectomy specimen.

She was then seen by me on  ___ with a plan to begin weekly
paclitaxel. She received 4 total doses of weekly paclitaxel
between ___ and ___ (4 doses total). She was then
admitted last ___ d/t report of urinary incontinence to rule
out a spinal
cord compression. 

She had imaging while in the hospital, which revealed extensive
skeletal involvement but no area of extension into the spinal
canal or to nerves.  As a result, she was not felt to be a
candidate for either surgical or radiotherapeutic intervention 
as
her disease was deemed widespread without identification of a

She was then referred for palliative XRT to the LS spine in 
___.

While receiving XRT to the LS spine and primarily while dealing
with complications of gastroparesis which required multiple,
short interval hospitalizations, Her repeat hospitalizations
focused primarily on pain control and gastroparesis symptoms. 
However, she also had closure of an ASD as a result of 
increasing
dyspnea and hypoxemia. 

As a result of all of this, she was unable to continue planned
chemotherapy following an unplanned  10 week treatment break as 
a
result of these complications.

Ultimately, a J-tube was placed and she is on tube feedings at

limits
this to the equivalent of one small meal per day.  She has been

intensity.  Multilevel disc desiccation and loss of disc height are seen.

narrowing.

mild right and no left foraminal narrowing.

mass effect on the right S1 and S2 nerve roots.  Unchanged large right

lumbar spine with multiple new lesions.

loss.

abdomen and pelvis following intravenous contrast administration.  A 3 minute
delayed scan through the abdomen was also acquired.
Oral contrast was administered.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.

mGy-cm.

22.4 mGy-cm.

mGy-cm.

mGy-cm.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Trace bilateral pleural effusions with bibasilar atelectasis.  No
pericardial effusion.

ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates homogenous attenuation throughout. 
Again seen are multiple scattered hepatic lesions, with decreased disease
burden compared to ___.  For instance, the largest lesion measures up
to 8 mm in the right hepatic lobe (05:12).  A vague infiltrative appearing
region in the right hepatic lobe measuring 3.9 x 2.6 cm has significantly
decreased in size since the prior study where it measured approximately 5.7 x
4.0 cm (05:21).  Gallbladder is surgically absent.  There is no biliary
dilation.

PANCREAS: Pancreas is mildly atrophic, but demonstrates homogeneous
attenuation throughout.  No focal lesions are identified.  There is no
pancreatic duct dilation.

SPLEEN: The spleen shows normal size and attenuation throughout, without
evidence of focal lesions.

ADRENALS: The right and left adrenal glands are normal in size and shape.

URINARY: The kidneys are of normal and symmetric size with normal nephrogram. 
There is a simple cyst in the lower pole of the right kidney that measures 4.2
x 3.3 cm.  No solid parenchymal lesions are identified.  No hydronephrosis on
either side.

GASTROINTESTINAL: There are postsurgical changes at the level of the
gastroesophageal junction.  Small bowel loops demonstrate normal caliber, wall
thickness, and enhancement throughout. The colon and rectum are within normal
limits. Tip of a percutaneous gastrostomy tube terminates in the distal
duodenum/proximal jejunum.

PELVIS: The urinary bladder and distal ureters are unremarkable.  There is no
free fluid in the pelvis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had terrible right back pain—up to a 10—and my right leg felt weak. Also, there’s this painful rash on my right side with big blisters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The rash—has it changed over time? Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. The blisters have been there for about three weeks. I’ve never had shingles, and this is the first time I’ve had a rash like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check it out. Given your history of metastatic breast cancer, we need to rule out infection or nerve involvement. We’ve started you on vancomycin and Zosyn just in case it’s a bacterial infection like bullous impetigo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it shingles? I’m worried it might be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. The rash is on one side and blistering, which fits. But we’re treating it cautiously until we get more info. We unroofed one blister for culture, but results will take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the back pain? It’s been sharp and constant. My leg felt weak when the pain was worst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your spine. It was a bit blurry because of movement, but we didn’t see any spinal cord compression. There is extensive bone metastasis, though, and some new lesions in your spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So the pain is from the cancer spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The metastases are contributing, and there’s also nerve root thickening. But no urgent compression, which is good. We’ve given you Dilaudid for pain and will keep adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My leg feels stronger now, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We also checked your chest and belly with X-rays. Your PICC line is in place, and your feeding tube is where it should be. No pneumonia or bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My J-tube has been acting up. I’ve had trouble with it clogging before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. The team is monitoring it. We may need to replace it if it’s not working. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and nutrition support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, maybe a 7 now. The meds help, but it’s not gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep working on it. Your labs are stable—no infection signs in blood. But your phosphate was low, so we’re replacing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the rash getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not spreading. We’re treating it as shingles with possible bacterial infection. We’ll continue antibiotics until we’re sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my feeding tube? I rely on that for nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace it tomorrow. The current one is clogged. We’ll put in a wider one to prevent future blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation. It’s a quick procedure. The new tube will have a larger lumen so it’s less likely to clog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the CT results. Your liver metastases have actually improved—fewer and smaller lesions. That’s a good sign your chemotherapy is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. But there are new bone spots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two new sclerotic lesions in the right pelvis. They could be new metastases. We’ll discuss with oncology, but no immediate intervention is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the rash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still consistent with shingles. We’re keeping you on antibiotics just in case there’s a bacterial infection on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit weak. Is it from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. You’ve been on IV fluids, but we know you’ve had malnutrition. That’s why replacing the feeding tube is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your feeding tube was successfully replaced this morning. It’s an 18 French tube, larger to prevent clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How soon can I start feeds again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow today—low rate, see how you tolerate it. We’ll use Osmolite 1.5, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? Are we still sure it’s shingles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still presuming shingles with possible bacterial complication. We’ll continue the antibiotics for now and reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is better—maybe a 5 now. Can I switch back to my home pain meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re already transitioning you back to Dilaudid and morphine. We’ll make sure you’re comfortable before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The feeding tube is working, and you’re tolerating nutrition. The rash is starting to scab over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled, you’re on the right meds, and home care is set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I continue chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oncologist wants you to resume paclitaxel on the 3-on, 1-off schedule. We’ll coordinate that through outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop the IV ones today. You’ll finish a course of oral vancomycin at home for the rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m anxious about managing everything at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a nurse to help with the tube and meds. And your DNR status is documented—we’ll respect your wishes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’ll discharge you this morning. Keep taking the vancomycin, use the pain meds as needed, and follow up with oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with metastatic ER+ breast cancer and a history of gastroparesis presented with severe right back pain, right lower extremity weakness, and a painful bullous rash on her right side. She was admitted for evaluation and management, with initial concern for shingles with possible bacterial superinfection, leading to treatment with intravenous vancomycin and Zosyn. MRI of the spine showed extensive metastatic bone disease without cord compression. A clogged G-J tube was successfully replaced with an 18 French tube to prevent recurrent blockages. She improved with pain control, nutritional support, and antibiotic therapy. The liver metastases showed decreased burden on CT, indicating response to prior chemotherapy. She was transitioned back to home pain medications, started on oral vancomycin, and discharged with plans to resume outpatient paclitaxel therapy and home nursing support.
